opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I look back, I don't think I was making these grand strategic decisions. A lot of it was being in the right place and following my curiosity at each step.

At SJTU, I was in an environment with a lot of very driven, very smart classmates, and that peer pressure, in a good way, pushed me to take research seriously early on. It was also where I first felt that computer vision was exciting. At that time, it wasn't the hottest thing in the world; deep learning hadn't really exploded yet. It just felt like a set of problems that were fun to think about: how do you get a machine to actually *see*?

Then for the PhD, going to UCSD was more about the people than the ranking or the brand. I think that's the most important thing for a PhD student: who you work with, and whether that person gives you the freedom to explore. I was lucky to have an advisor who let me try things, fail, and figure out my own taste in research. And the timing was interesting, because right when I started, deep learning was taking off. Everything was changing so fast, and being in a place that wasn't overly rigid let me jump into that wave.

So if there's a lesson, it's that I'd rather optimize for the environment and the people than for prestige. A lot of the things that mattered most for me, like collaborators, internships, and the ideas that eventually turned into papers, came out of those relationships, not out of a carefully planned career path.

r002.rationale: He describes following his curiosity and adapting to changes in research, but does not state that he is willing to grow alongside the institutions he joins.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I was ever that strategic about it. When I was at Shanghai Jiao Tong I was in the ACM class, and at that point I barely knew what research was. I just knew I liked solving problems, and that environment pushed you very hard on fundamentals, on algorithms and coding. Looking back, that training mattered a lot more than I realized at the time, because it gave me the ability to actually build things rather than just talk about ideas.

Going to UCSD for my PhD was partly luck and partly instinct. I wanted to work on computer vision, and Zhuowen Tu was there doing work I found really interesting, sitting at the intersection of vision and learning. It wasn't the most famous place, and some people asked me why I didn't aim for a bigger name, but I think picking an advisor you can genuinely work with matters more than the ranking of the school. San Diego was also a bit removed from the hype, which was good for me. There was space to think, to read, to try things that failed. That's where I started working on deep learning seriously, around the time it was taking off, and I got to be close enough to the center of the field to feel the energy but far enough to not just follow the crowd.

So if there's a pattern, it's probably that I chose people and problems over prestige, and I trusted that if the work was good, the rest would follow. I still tell my students the same thing now.

r001.rationale: He describes choosing UCSD for its advisor and environment, but does not say he can recognize an institution’s potential for future growth.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think those choices were a combination of curiosity, opportunity, and a little bit of chance. It’s easy to tell a very coherent story afterward, as though I knew exactly where each step would lead, but that’s not really how these decisions feel at the time.

For me, the important question is: Will this environment help me grow? Are there people I can learn from, and will I have room to discover what I actually want to work on? That’s how I would frame the choices around SJTU and UCSD—as steps toward learning more about both the field and myself, rather than parts of a plan I had figured out from the beginning.

r001.rationale: He asks whether an environment will help him grow, but does not say he can recognize an institution’s potential for future growth.

r002.rationale: He describes SJTU and UCSD as steps in his own learning and growth, not as institutions he is willing to grow alongside.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about those choices as choosing an environment where I can grow. You never have complete information when you make a decision like that, so I wouldn’t describe it as a perfectly planned path. You have some interests, you see an opportunity, and you take a step. Then what you learn changes how you think about the next step.

For me, the useful questions are: What can I learn here? Who can I learn from? And will this environment help me discover what I actually want to work on? That’s how I would frame choices like SJTU and UCSD.
